tagline.text: Free state cars of past presidents at Quezon Circle

location.label: Location
location.text: Inside Quezon Memorial Circle (Elliptical Road), Quezon City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0~500 (free admission; transport and meals included, per person)

children.text: Run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) inside Quezon Memorial Circle, this museum shows 12 restored cars used by 13 past presidents, plus a children's road safety gallery, with no admission fee. It is open Tuesday to Sunday.

The Presidential Car Museum (Filipino name: Museo ng Pampangulong Sasakyan) is a small museum inside Quezon Memorial Circle park in Quezon City. It is run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). Plans were reported around 2013, ground was broken in 2017, and it was formally inaugurated on
August 19, 2018

. Quezon City provided at least 3,000 sq m under an agreement with the NHCP, and the basketball and volleyball courts that stood there were moved elsewhere in the park. It is described as the largest collection of historic state cars in the Philippines, so it is a worthwhile stop at Quezon Circle for anyone interested in Philippine history.

The core of the display is the official cars that past presidents actually rode in. They were once kept in a private warehouse in Pampanga and were restored before being gathered here. There are 12 cars used by 13 presidents, running from Emilio Aguinaldo of the First Republic to Gloria Macapagal Arroyo. A kalesa carriage from the early 20th century and a World War II-era jeep sit alongside them, so even if you are not a car enthusiast it is a fun way to skim modern Philippine history by its vehicles. Note that President Carlos P. Garcia's car was never recovered and is not on display, and one report said President Benigno Aquino III's car was still in use at the time, so the lineup may change over time.

In December 2024 the museum reopened after several months of repairs, with a new children's road safety gallery, the TASK Central Hub (Tamang Asal Sa Kalsada), supported by the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and San Miguel Holdings Corporation (SMHC). Today you can enjoy the classic cars and a hands-on road safety experience for kids in a single visit.

There is no admission fee and the exhibits are indoors, so it is an easy stop that keeps you out of Manila's midday heat and sudden showers. Several other sights sit in the same park, including the Quezon museum and the Quezon Heritage House, so it fits well as one stop in a half-day itinerary. Just allow for the walk from the park entrance to the museum.

Aguinaldo's 1924 Packard Single Six Touring, Quezon's 1937 Chrysler Airflow Custom Imperial CW, Marcos's 1980 Lincoln Continental Mark VI and others used by 13 presidents are arranged in chronological order. Each car has a note on who rode in it and when. Starting from the carriage, through the 1920s Packard, to the Lincolns and Mercedes-Benz of the 1980s, you can see at a glance how state cars changed with the times.

The 1930s Cadillac V-16 is presented as a car that President Quezon used and then handed to General Douglas MacArthur in 1937. It shows the relationship between the Philippines and the United States since colonial times through a single car. Be sure to read the label for when it was used.

This jeep was donated by MacArthur and is said to have been used by Ramon Magsaysay while he was Secretary of National Defense (1950–1953). It is a small vehicle that recalls the mood of the postwar Philippines.
The 1960 Rolls-Royce Phantom V is presented as a car owned by Imelda Marcos from 1965 to 1986. It stands out because it was a first lady's personal car shown alongside the presidents' cars.

A kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) once used by the family of León Apacible, a member of the commission that drafted the Malolos Constitution, is on display. You can see a ceremonial ride from before the age of the automobile.

An interactive wall display pointing out the parts of a state car, an audio-visual room and a souvenir shop help you understand the safety features of presidential vehicles. It is designed so that visitors curious about how a presidential car differs from an ordinary one can grasp it easily.

blocks.title: TASK Central Hub road safety gallery

children.text: On a small mock street you can practice pedestrian crossings, traffic lights and parking areas, and you can see a QR code listing traffic signs and comic-style etiquette boards. It suits families with children and school field trips.
Arrive at opening time and follow the entrance guidance. Sources differ between 8:00 and 9:00 AM, so arriving after
is the safe choice.
In the exhibition hall, look at the cars in chronological order from Aguinaldo to Arroyo. Reading the notes beside each car takes about
40 minutes
Take a look at the interactive wall, the audio-visual room and the souvenir shop.
If you are with children, try the road safety experience at the TASK Central Hub.
The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday,
to
, so an afternoon visit also works, but morning is recommended because the park is less hot.
Stroll from the park entrance toward the Quezon Memorial Shrine.
Learn about President Quezon's life at the Quezon museum beneath the shrine.
Walk to the Presidential Car Museum and view the state cars.
Have lunch and rest at a restaurant or the food park inside the park.
Finish with the remaining museums, such as the Quezon Heritage House or Bahay Modernismo.
Each museum has slightly different hours. Most are closed on Mondays, so plan your visit for Tuesday to Sunday.

items.title: From Manila by metro and jeepney

children.text: From Makati or Pasay, take MRT-3 and get off at Quezon Avenue station.
In front of the station, board a jeepney bound for Philcoa, get off along Elliptical Road, and walk about

to the park (per one travel guide; it varies with where you get off, so check locally). Tell the driver beforehand to drop you at "Quezon Memorial Circle" or "City Hall", and if you get off at City Hall, enter the park through the pedestrian underpass. The museum is closest to the park's Commonwealth-side gate.
North Avenue station is also fairly close, but check the exact distance locally.
The MRT-7 Quezon Memorial Circle station is under construction. Check the latest announcements for its opening date.
Enter "Quezon Memorial Circle" as your destination. Choosing "Quezon Memorial Shrine" shortens the walk if you want to be dropped off near the museum.
A spacious parking area in front of the museum is mentioned. Check the park's parking fee locally.
Elliptical Road is busy at rush hour, so leave extra time.
Take the Carousel bus along the EDSA busway, get off at the Quezon Avenue stop and transfer to a jeepney.
Because the exhibits are indoors, you can visit in the rain and at any time of year. However, there is a lot of walking in the park with little shade, so the weather still matters.
The museum is closed on Mondays. Weekend mornings are crowded with locals exercising in the park and visiting families, and weekday mornings are the quietest.

The museum itself has no lodging, and most visitors come as a day trip from Makati, BGC or central Manila. If you want to stay in Quezon City, business and mid-range hotels between MRT North Avenue and Quezon Avenue stations are convenient, with many options around Vertis North and Eton Centris.

For food, use the restaurants and food park inside the park, or the eateries around nearby Quezon Avenue and Timog Avenue. It is polite not to bring food into the museum. A simple plan is to snack while walking the park paths after the museum and have lunch in the restaurant areas of Quezon City. Because opening hours end at
, avoid a late-afternoon visit.
The museum is closed on Mondays. It is listed as open
to
Tuesday to Sunday, but some sources say it opens at 8 AM, so check social media and NHCP notices.
Admission is free so it is easy to drop in, but reading the labels takes time, so set aside at least
1 hour
If you are with children, see the TASK Central Hub first, then move on to the state cars before the kids get bored.

Groups and school field trips can book. The inquiry email is pcm@nhcp.gov.ph. Phone numbers differ by source (a 2025 article lists (+63) 905 435 3396, the Quezon City listing 0919-469-6987), so confirm by email before you go.
Pairing the Quezon museum (beneath the shrine) and the Quezon Heritage House on the same day is efficient. Each museum has different hours.
Photography rules may differ by gallery, so ask a staff member first.
There is little shade in the park, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and spend the midday hours in the indoor exhibits.
If someone asks for a fee on the elevated walkway or elsewhere in the park, note that in February 2026 the city said such fees were not legitimate, so do not pay. Check the official fees locally.
Car enthusiasts should photograph the model year and period of use on each label. Matching them with a timeline of Philippine presidents later is fun.
Car positions and order can change, so the surest way is to ask staff at the entrance about the current lineup.
Hours and exhibits change often. Check the official NHCP announcements before visiting.
Sources differ on opening time, 8 AM or 9 AM. You may arrive early and find it closed, so we recommend arriving after 9 AM.
The car list is based on 2021 material, so exhibits may have been rotated.
Park redevelopment and MRT-7 construction may block or relocate some paths.
Avoid food and loud voices in the museum, and do not touch the cars.
Parts of the park may close temporarily during typhoons or heavy rain.
Phone numbers and email addresses can change over time, so also check the latest posts on the official Facebook page.
The park that houses the museum. It has the 66 m Quezon Memorial Shrine, the Quezon museum below it and walking paths.

blocks.title: Quezon Memorial Shrine and Quezon museum

children.text: Located beneath the shrine at the center of the park, with the tomb of President Quezon and his wife and an exhibit on his life.
Another history exhibit inside the park. Check the opening hours locally.
To see the presidential residence you need to travel into central Manila, about
40 minutes to 1 hour
by car.
